assessment: The cited2020 study establishes price-response evidence; subtracting consumer pass-through from100does not identify owner gains. The related four-recipient primary study expressly assigns separate shares to workers and suppliers, and estimates owners57.7/62.4/55.7percent at6/18/30months (counterfactual-price variants62.9/65.9/59.1). The author presents80percent as an ownership allocation, not merely a producer-side remainder. This supports a narrow source-description correction.
strongest_alternatives: The2019study explicitly treats estimated owner gains as a lower bound, owing to potentially overstated employee/material effects and price-data scope. Actual80percent is not ruled out; avoid saying actual gains were necessarily55.7percent.

Owners may be loose shorthand for the entire non-consumer producer side. Explicit ownership wording and the separate recipient groups make this inaccurate as a description of the cited research, while the broad low-pass-through conclusion remains supported.
The2020and2019papers have different research questions and estimators. The2019numbers must not be presented as an exact corrected estimate from the cited2020paper.
materiality: Minor: the ownership concentration is exaggerated as a research attribution, but owners remain the largest group, consumers receive little and the targeting objection survives.
direction: True for the distributional rationale against the VAT cut: attributing the entire non-consumer share to owners makes the subsidy seem more concentrated. This does not prove the policy recommendation wrong.
